# pyforai — A DSH plugin that adds a checkable, addressable structure to Python
English | 中文
> pyforai is a DSH plugin for Python AI coding agents. Comment anchors are validated by `check` and
used as block handles by `wrap` / `replace-body` / `move`.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Python's parser ignores `# end if` / `# end for` entirely. That is the point: **no new syntax, no co
rpus lost**. But `pyforai` compares every anchor against the AST — a mismatch is a hard error.
That maps to two layers:
- **L1 `check`** treats anchors as assertions: it verifies them against the indentation, and the dia

gnostic names the kind and line it expects.
- **L2 `wrap` / `replace-body` / `move`** treats anchors
as handles for structural edits, handling indentation automatically so the model no longer does whi
structural edits, handling indentation automatically so the model no longer does whitespace surgery.
## DSH plugin
A structural editing and validation tool for Python AI coding. pyforai uses comment anchors to give
Python code a checkable structural representation, solving the indentation drift and structural-tran
sformation problems of AI coding. As a DSH plugin it exposes `pyforai_check` and `pyforai_edit` as t
wo native tools, with `wrap`, `replace-body`, and `move` operations, so an AI agent can generate or
refactor Python without hand-editing whitespace.
`dsh-plugin/` itself is a Host-only DSH bundle:
[该节后续省略]
## What this project set out to do
pyforai did not start as a Python tool; it started as an exploration of a **language for AI programm
ing**: if the primary reader is a model rather than a human, what should the syntax look like?
Python was the starting point because of corpus richness — models have seen the most of it and write
it best, and any new syntax would trade that prior away. The cost is that Python's indentation was
designed for humans and is machine-hostile. The obvious move is a Python dialect, for example `{}` i
nstead of indentation — but that immediately loses compatibility with existing Python: parsers, form
atters, linters, tests, and all existing code would have to change.
So the compromise is **comment anchors + tooling enforcement**: zero syntax change, no corpus lost;
structural information lives in comments the parser already ignores, and `check` plus structural edi
ting turn it into something checkable and addressable. This is an engineering compromise, not the op
timal language design — and its ceiling comes from exactly this trade-off (see "What it solves, and
what it doesn't" below).
## Why comments, not braces or a new dialect
Indentation has two real problems:
1. **Block structure is not addressable** — the token stream has no block boundaries and no names, s

o blocks can only be referred to by line number or text snippet.
2. **Structural changes are not loc
al** — wrapping a block in `try` / `if` reindents the whole section, inflating the diff and drifting
ng a block in `try` / `if` reindents the whole section, inflating the diff and drifting indentation.
Braces fix both halves at once, but the price is losing corpus and breaking toolchains. Comment anch
ors fix only the first half; the second half comes from structural editing (`wrap` / `replace-body`
/ `move`). That is why the approach is cheap, and why its ceiling is limited.
Three reasons for choosing Python all point at "don't touch the syntax":
- **Rich corpus**: any syntax extension trades prior knowledge for structure. Comments are the only

channel in Python that is expressive yet completely ignored by the parser — zero syntax delta.
- **G
lue, with room to sink**: Python is the orchestration layer with dense control flow — exactly where

dedent semantics concentrate. Core modules can still move down to C/Rust/Go.
- **Fast feedback**: bu
t silent indentation errors bypass it — the syntax is valid, tests may not cover it, and a formatter
can freeze the wrong structure. Anchors pull those errors back into fast feedback.
## What it solves, and what it doesn't
| | Role of the anchor | Strength |

| Generation | One explicit commitment when closing a block; less "stack loss" | Weakly positive |
|

Editing | Anchors alone do not reindent; pair them with `wrap` / `replace-body` / `move` | None |
|

Validation | Turns "intent vs tokens" divergence into a detectable error | Medium |
| Representatio
n | Blocks get handles: wrap/replace/move, searchable, reviewable | Strong |
One limitation must be stated clearly: **an anchor is a second sample of the same intent, not an ind
ependent checksum.** If the author's understanding of the structure and the indentation are wrong in
the same place, the anchor is wrong in the same place too. It catches drift, not systematic misunde
rstanding. That is still valuable — drift dominates indentation incidents — but do not treat it as a
t is still valuable — drift dominates indentation incidents — but do not treat it as a formal proof.
## What `fmt` is for (important)
[代码示例省略，未执行]
`fmt` does exactly one thing: insert anchors into blocks that **have none**.
- Insertion is inner-first; nested blocks ending on the same line are ordered by descending column,

so the file reads inside-out.
- If the file already contains **invalid** anchors, `fmt` refuses to r

un. That is deliberate: silently "fixing" an assertion hides the bug it was meant to expose.
- **`fm
t` inserts an AST mirror, not an assertion.** It improves readability and gives editors handles, but
adds no validation value — it sees the same tree as the parser. Real validation value comes from wr
iting anchors first and letting `check` compare them.
## Limitations (v0.1)
- No clause-level anchors (an `# end if` before `else`). `else`/`elif`/`except`/`finally`/`case` are

already explicit boundary tokens.
- Cannot replace a `match` body, or move a block into `match`.
-

Only compound statements can be moved, not single simple statements.
- move does no semantic checks

(scope, imports, control flow).
- No blank-line/style normalization; run a formatter after large cha

nges.
- Anchors are not an independent checksum (see "second sample" above).
